*This blog post is based on John Kibarian’s, CEO & Co-Founder, PDF Solutions,*[executive keynote at PDF Solutions CONNECT 2026](https://www.pdf.com/users-conference/connect-2026/next-generation-pdf-solutions-platform-for-the-global-semiconductor-industry/)


When John Kibarian opened CONNECT 2026 in San Francisco last month, he told the room it was the most exciting time he has seen in three decades in the semiconductor industry. Not because the industry is in an upcycle (it always overshoots, he reminded the audience), but because AI is changing how the industry operates, not just what it sells.


That shift comes with a price. In a world where you cannot get more tools than you have already been promised, the only way to meet demand is to get more out of everything you have. Kibarian framed that pressure as three efficiency challenges:


1. **Energy efficiency:** getting more out of the AI data centers being built.
2. **Data and compute efficiency:** using AI to create insights from manufacturing data at an acceptable cost.
3. **Supply chain efficiency:** operating a globally distributed, increasingly complex supply chain.


## Part 1: The energy efficiency challenge


**Q: Why is AI is a bigger transformation for the semiconductor industry than mobile or the internet?**


Mobile and the internet changed what we sold. We built a lot of new things, but they didn’t change how the industry operates. AI does both. It is driving the demand, and at the same time it is changing the way we analyze data, the way we run factories, and the way companies collaborate across the supply chain. We started thinking about this about four years ago, when ChatGPT appeared. Michael Yu, who runs our Advanced Solutions group, sent around an email asking how we would reimagine everything we do around analytics assuming it is all AI-first. What you are seeing at PDF Solutions CONNECT this year is our answer.


**Q: Based on current projections, how big is the growth of the semiconductor industry ?**


When SEMI first said the industry would be a trillion dollars by 2030, most industry insiders were incredulous. It wouldn’t happen on that schedule: it happened years earlier. Looking forward, McKinsey’s base case takes device revenue from $975 billion in 2025 to about $2.3 trillion in 2030, an 83.5% increase in volume, and 58% of that growth comes from data center and server. Whether there is a downturn before or after 2030 can be debated, but they always happen.


**Q: What does the semiconductor revenue projection means in terms of manufacturing capacity?**


Installed AI data center capacity is around 45–60 gigawatts today. Our estimate is that doubles to triples by 2030; some people say six times. At 150,000–200,000 wafers per gigawatt, half of it HBM, that is 9.6 to 17.5 million additional wafers and 16 to 29 new fabs. This fab number is conservative, because it assumes 50,000 wafer starts a month. Nobody builds a 50K fab at the leading edge anymore. A leading-edge logic fab is more like 20K. You could easily double that number.


**Q: Is the growth of the semiconductor manufacturing capacity over the next few years mainly a capex problem?**


That is what it looks like from the outside. Nation states look at the numbers and decide they can write the check. Those who have been inside a fab know it is a lot more than putting in orders for capital. New fab construction is not enough. The challenge is getting more compute out of the data centers being built. Richard Feynman laid out the fundamental limits of computing in the 1980s, and by his numbers we are still about a factor of a million away.[There is a lot of room at the top of the stack and a lot of room at the bottom.](https://www.pdf.com/users-conference/connect-2026/whats-next-for-computing/)


**Q: What are the ways the semiconductor can use to help create additional efficiency from the AI data centers?**


New designs, for one. For most of our history, new customers came from Asia, because that is where fabs and fabless companies were being started. Now every foundation model company and every data center provider is doing its own chip, and one the key goal for these new chips is energy efficiency. Each new accelerator generation is claiming about twice the energy efficiency of the last. Workloads are being tuned too. Training keeps a chip saturated at its design point. A GPU doing inference can spend over 90% of its power on memory and idle. There is a lot to be had there.


**Q: What do the new AI chips designs mean for the people who manufacture and test them?**


A proliferation of bespoke designs. Smaller production volumes across many more products. Much wider datasets, with test programs in the millions of test items. Customers almost never leave NPI anymore; the breadth of what they test in NPI carries straight through manufacturing. And a much more complex assembly and test supply chain, with test information passing up and down the chain to create more product grades. Down-binning used to be a flash memory thing. Now it is happening across many product categories. Add new technologies like co-packaged optics, where you have more than electrons moving around, and you have a set of problems where silicon lifecycle intelligence matters more than ever.


**Q: It is often said that nowadays fabless companies have become manufacturers. Why and what does it really mean?**


For years fabless customers said that they couldn’t spend much on manufacturing software because they weren’t manufacturers. They ordered wafers, the foundry tested at sort, package yields were 99%. Now the joke is: you have all become manufacturers. For complex hybrid packages, what happens after the wafer leaves the front-end fab is where a lot of the action is in our industry today.


**Q: How is PDF Solutions helping semiconductor companies develop new and more efficient chips?**


Everything that was presented at[PDF Solutions CONNECT](https://www.pdf.com/users-conference/connect-2026/) is about getting more out of the manufacturing process. With DirectScan™ and the Characterization Vehicle®, we are using more design information to know where and how to look at sub-7nm nodes, including e-beam techniques that charge nodes and sense other nodes in the design. With Exensio®, we have moved analysis from the client to a Python-first, natively parallel compute engine built for very wide datasets. To steal a headline from one of the[technical sessions](https://www.pdf.com/users-conference/connect-2026/pdf-solutions-platform-architecture-overview-and-new-solutions-announcements/) : anywhere from 20 to 40x what you would get spending the same dollars on hardware, because we make much more efficient use of the cores. On top of that we integrate AI and agents to drive the analytics. It is hard to imagine 10 million parameters. It is not hard for an algorithm. And with Sapience® and Exensio Process Control, we extend process control and orchestration across the supply chain. The goal is to solve the dark data problem: agents at work on 100% of the data, 24/7.


## Part 2: The data and compute efficiency challenge


**Q: Recently it was said that AI only became useful in the last six months. What would that mean for the semiconductor industry? And how would we know?**


AI has been useful a little longer than that. But it is an interesting perspective coming after the industry has already crossed a trillion dollars. The right question for us is: what does useful mean for semiconductor manufacturing? I think it means four things. Combining common-knowledge industry data with company-specific data. Efficiently using all the manufacturing data you have. Managing the compute cost of AI for ongoing analysis. And deploying agents at the manufacturing edge, across applications and the supply chain. Every one of those is harder than it looks.


**Q: How much do large language models already understand about the semiconductor industry?**


A lot. Wafer maps, parametric test, bins, lots, SPC charts, etch-rate drift, failure mechanisms. They reason well, they pick methods, they write code, they interpret results, they summarize unstructured data. If you tell one you have a yield loss in your lots and ask what analysis to run, you get a pretty decent first pass. About what a junior engineer would propose.


**Q: What is missing from what LLM can do for semiconductor manufacturing?**


Everything the senior engineer has in their head. The junior engineer runs the analysis, sees a signal they can’t explain, decides it is garbage and tells you there is nothing in the data. The senior engineer looks at the same chart and says, what do you mean, it is obvious what is going on here. That is because they know that tool is a four-chamber tool with two identical chambers, so they know what pattern to look for. They know that 50,000 part numbers collapse into a few families, like 32 variations on a theme, and they know when to lump the data together. LLMs miss company-specific data and IP, the historical baseline, product and process specifics like recipes, design rules, test flows and bin definitions, very large volumes of statistical computation, and validation.


**Q: Semiconductor manufacturing creates and stores a lot of data. In most cases all the data needed to prevent most yield crashes was already there. Why isn’t it used?**


In many yield crash situations, when you go back and look, the data was almost always there. But there are a million signals in any facility, and when you look at test data there are always a million things that look a bit strange. You can’t decide which ones are relevant until you know you have an event. Then you look back and say, oh, I guess that was relevant. Getting efficient with wide datasets is how you react before the crash instead of explaining it afterward.


**Q: What is the magnitude of the semiconductor manufacturing challenge?**


Fabless and giga-scale foundry customers have petabytes per site, across 20-plus data domains with 100-plus file formats each. A new 3D-IC has somewhere between two and ten million parameters at NPI. Even the mixed-signal companies with only 10,000 test parameters are sitting on about 200 terabytes of analytics data. All of them have more products than employees, let alone product and test engineers. One leading foundry describes analyzing two to three trillion sort parameters across about 2,000 products every week. The most important factor in using AI in semiconductor manufacturing is accessing and processing that kind of extremely complex private data.


**Q: What does PDF Solutions bring to the challenge of analyzing very large semiconductor data sets?**


Thirty years of semiconductor manufacturing knowledge, which is what gives AI its context. We manage petabytes for our customers, almost all on isolated cloud sites. Your data is not swimming with everyone else’s, and neither are your agents. We have taped out about a thousand test chips at 28nm and below in the last 15 years and analyzed every one of them, which refines our models. Our customers have built about 660,000 analysis templates across those sites. And we have a very extensive ontology for how to align and collect semiconductor data. That is the foundation we built Exensio Aurora on.


**Q: It is often said that tokens are now one of the single biggest IT expense. How does that shape the way we think about the role of LLMs and AI in the analysis of semiconductor manufacturing data?**


At PDF Solutions tokens are our most expensive IT line item and it is growing fast. When we put caps on developer tokens, an engineer came to me at two in the afternoon and said, I’m out of tokens, I might as well go home, because I can’t finish in five hours without them and I can do it in five minutes tomorrow. We gave him the tokens. But it tells you how much has changed, and it tells you the cost is real. And manufacturing has a particular problem with that cost, because a lot of what we do is repetitive by design. If you are in automotive, you want to screen parts the same way for 25 years so you are auditable. You do not want hallucinations.


**Q: How can illustrate the token cost impact on semiconductor manufacturing data analysis?**


Say you want to repeatedly analyze a 100,000-row, 10-column data sample. If you pull the data out through the APIs and have an LLM run the analysis, it is about 30,000 tokens just to make a chart, roughly 30 watt-hours, every single time. If instead you ask the LLM to build a workflow, a query as a Python block, a plot as a Python block, an annotation on top, it takes about 20,000 tokens the first time. Then you store that workflow. The next time, you use the workflow since it exists, and it runs at about 0.02 watt-hours. A thousandth of the energy. For repeatable analytical tasks, LLMs do not give you economies of scale. Workflows do.


**Q: So how does Exensio Aurora use LLMs?**


Our conclusion was that LLMs need a language, and the language is Python, expressed as workflows stored in a library. The approach has four parts. First, align and enrich the data with a semiconductor ontology. Second, run the analysis on a highly scalable compute engine designed for semiconductor data. Third, use the LLM to create workflows and agents. That is just writing code, which is what LLMs are great at. Fourth, use the workflows to encode context and repeatable analysis. The engineer doesn’t read lines of Python; they look at workflow blocks, execute them, and if they like the result, they say generalize that and store it so they can use it again. Next time, just run the workflow and save me the 20,000 tokens.


**Q: Why is the way LLM are used in Exensio Aurora secure?**


It air-gaps the data from the LLM. Customers can try different models, including ones that aren’t on premise, without their data leaving the premises. And because the knowledge is captured in workflows you can go back and inspect, you prevent hallucinations. Satya Nadella said something in October that captures it well: “securing AI means separating the model from the harness that orchestrates its work and externalizing the controls and safeguards. That is exactly what Aurora does. It gives you predictability, repeatability and cost efficiency.”


## Part 3: The supply chain efficiency challenge


**Q: Why does the semiconductor supply chain belong in a conversation about AI and efficiency?**


Because in the world of hybrid packages, all manufacturing is a complex supply chain execution problem. Wafer fabrication, die preparation, wafer bonding, die stacking, TSV and interconnect, advanced packaging, test and metrology: each of those can happen at a different site, run by different companies, in a different country. Material moves around a lot. And the dirty little secret of reshoring fabs is that we haven’t reshored assembly and test. So the wafer gets finished here and flies somewhere else anyway, and it goes through many places before it becomes a product.


**Q: Is the globalization of the semiconductor supply chain the reason why PDF Solutions acquired secureWISE?**


Exactly. secureWISE was the largest network between fabs and equipment vendors, in virtually every 3nm fab in the world with a handful of exceptions. It transmits nearly exabytes of data between the equipment vendors and the fabs. A number of equipment vendors’ AI solutions are built on it. They collect data across their fleet, drive learning, and push algorithms back to the tools.


**Q: What makes secureWISE different from any other secure connection?**


Control. It is double-encrypted, so we never see what is inside the packets. The factory team has tremendous control over what data comes out, when it comes out, what data and algorithms come back in, what virus scans run on anything entering the factory, and there is a long audit trail of everything. That is what fabs demand, and it is what fabless companies and OSATs are going to need as they take on more of the manufacturing problem. We are bringing it out to the rest of our community now.


**Q: Collaboration in the semiconductor industry is described as becoming agentic. What does that look like?**


The semiconductor industry has always run on collaboration, and historically that collaboration happened between people. secureWISE started as a way for humans to collaborate without getting on airplanes. But if you look at the vast majority of the traffic on the network, and the majority of the revenue associated with it, it is data moving out and software or algorithms coming back. It is already more driven by agents and AI than by humans. That is where the whole industry is going, and it means interconnecting the industry more tightly, in a structured way, becomes increasingly important.


**Q: How does all of this fit together as a platform – the PDF Solutions platform?**


The same stack repeats wherever the work happens. In new-product development, in the fab, and at supply chain partners like OSATs, you have Exensio Aurora and enterprise applications integrated with Sapience, with apps and agents on top. In the factory, Cimetrix connects the equipment, including eProbe, to the manufacturing systems and the enterprise data warehouse. And secureWISE provides secure edge deployment and control across all of it, so data, rules, workflows and agents can move between sites under the control of the people who own the data.


## One platform, connected intelligence


**Q: Last question. If someone remembers one thing from the keynote, what should it be?**


That efficiency is the whole game now. Whether the downturn comes before 2030 or after it, our customers are going to be asked to get more compute out of every megawatt, more insight out of every token and every core, and more out of a supply chain that moves data and algorithms between agents as securely as it used to move people between sites. We have spent 30 years helping this industry ramp yield, apply the latest IT technology to manufacturing data, and connect operations across the supply chain. In the AI era, those three things matter more than ever, and they matter most when they run on one platform. That is what the next generation of the PDF Solutions platform is built to do.


*John Kibarian delivered his executive keynote, “Next Generation PDF Solutions Platform for the Global Semiconductor Industry,” at PDF Solutions CONNECT 2026 on October 15 in San Francisco. Industry figures cited in this post are drawn from McKinsey & Company and Omdia (2026 base case), SemiAnalysis, IBS 2026 and the SEMI 300mm Fab Report 2026.*
